pages.title: The enduring Emirates edge
pages.why: The deck's cover

pages.title: Emirates has the strongest all-round Gulf system today, conditional on Dubai, yield and aircraft
pages.why: The opening states the answer and the four conditions it rests on, with the evidence for each pillar in one table

pages.title: Only the March-year passenger lead is a like-for-like Emirates-Qatar comparison
pages.why: Five possible Emirates-Qatar comparisons are each judged on one test, whether the two numbers share a boundary, and the pattern of failures is the finding

pages.title: The rival set spans established hubs, Saudi growth and low-cost feeders
pages.why: The reader has to recognise six named carriers, the system each runs and its scale before the comparison starts

pages.title: 01 / The earnings engine
pages.why: Section structure

pages.title: Emirates now earns a 15% margin, against 1-3% before the pandemic
pages.why: Revenue and margin broke from their pre-pandemic range together, and each needs its own scale to show it

pages.title: Passengers and seat capacity both remain about 9% below their FY19 peaks
pages.why: Volume has two measures - passengers carried and seats flown - and the claim holds only if both sit below FY19 together

pages.title: Yield outgrew unit cost, cutting the breakeven load factor from 66% to 54%
pages.why: The margin is the end of a chain - yield against unit cost sets the breakeven load, and the gap to the actual load is the margin - so each link is its own exhibit, read left to right

pages.title: Operating profit rose only AED0.5bn as staff and other costs absorbed the gains
pages.why: The claim is what the year's change in operating profit is made of, five reconciled drivers between two totals

pages.title: Employee costs rose 64% in ten years, faster than fuel, to a record share
pages.why: The claim is how the cost base is made up and which part grew fastest over ten years, so the four parts are stacked by year

pages.title: Net debt fell from AED92.5bn to AED1.3bn as cash rose to match borrowings
pages.why: The claim is how far the balance sheet has turned since the pandemic, so cash and debt are drawn side by side for ten years

pages.title: Average fleet age doubled to 10.8 years; capital spending is at a ten-year high
pages.why: Renewal is the claim: the fleet's rising age and the spending that has only now resumed are two measures of it, each on its own scale

pages.title: Today's fleet is A380s and 777s; 270 of 367 aircraft on order are 777X
pages.why: Renewal is a move from one fleet to another, so the aircraft flying today and the aircraft on order are read left to right

pages.title: Cargo tonnage is back to 2.4 million, still 10% below its FY19 peak
pages.why: Cargo's recovery is a ten-year shape - a pre-pandemic peak, a collapse and a slow climb back - marked where it happens

pages.title: 02 / The Dubai network
pages.why: Section structure

pages.title: Dubai stayed the world's busiest international airport in 2025, 15 million ahead of Heathrow
pages.why: Where Dubai stands among the world's international airports is the claim, so the whole top ten is ranked for two years with Dubai marked

pages.title: Dubai traffic is 10% above 2019; Doha's is 40% and Abu Dhabi's 53% above
pages.why: Whether Dubai's growth leads or lags is settled only by setting it against every comparable hub from the same base year

pages.title: Saudi Arabia is Dubai's second-largest market at 7.5 million, traffic Saudi hubs now target
pages.why: The Saudi market is read twice - by country among Dubai's ten largest, and by city among its five largest - and the two cuts together show how much is at stake

pages.title: Five long-haul examples show the spread of a 152-city network from one hub
pages.why: Where the network reaches is the claim, so five long-haul examples are drawn from the single hub

pages.title: Africa grew revenue 9.7% as the Americas shrank; Europe and East Asia earn 59%
pages.why: The claim has two cuts of the same six regions - where the revenue is and how fast each moved in the year - read side by side

pages.title: Partnerships extend Emirates reach well beyond its 152 operated cities
pages.why: Partnership reach is a structure - operated cities at the centre, partners extending access around them - so it is drawn as one

pages.title: flydubai adds 15.7 million short-haul passengers that feed Dubai's long-haul banks
pages.why: flydubai's contribution has four parallel parts - passengers, flights, destinations and joint flow - each with its own number and meaning

pages.title: Dubai dropped from 15th to 31st among world megahubs yet still leads its region
pages.why: Where Dubai sits in the whole field of world megahubs is the claim, so the top forty are sorted on OAG's index and Dubai marked

pages.title: Al Maktoum is a planned capacity release, not part of today's lead
pages.why: One planned number - Al Maktoum's first phase - carries the claim, set against DXB's traffic today so the reader sees it is future capacity, not current

pages.title: The 2026 shock hit Dubai hardest: its September seats are still 15% down
pages.why: The shock and its uneven recovery only read together: Dubai's own traffic fall, then the seats each Gulf airline and airport has put back

pages.title: 03 / The customer proposition
pages.why: Section structure

pages.title: Premium Economy is now a visible, bookable part of the Emirates brand
pages.why: The claim is that the cabin is visible and bookable, so the reader should see the product before its scale

anchors.photo: Emirates A350 electric Premium Economy seat with cabin crew, September 2026

pages.title: 104 aircraft are retrofitted, 47% of a 219-aircraft cabin programme
pages.why: One number carries the claim - retrofits done against the programme - with the other cabin counts beside it for scale

pages.title: Emirates flies 116 A380s, nearly ten times the next operator's fleet
pages.why: The claim is Emirates' place among every A380 operator, so all ten are ranked with Emirates marked

pages.title: The A350 is a second renewal path, already flying while the 777X waits
pages.why: Cabin and fleet renewal has two paths, compared on the same terms: what is flying, what is ordered and when it arrives

pages.title: Emirates slipped from 4th to 6th on Skytrax as Saudia and Etihad climbed
pages.why: Ranks are positions, not quantities, so they are read down a table in 2026 order with the move beside each, rather than drawn on a value axis

pages.title: Qatar wins the 2026 premium-service awards; Emirates wins the middle cabin
pages.why: Six award measures are read across for the two carriers, the leader of each drawn as its mark, and the split between premium and middle-cabin wins is the finding

pages.title: The new A350 seat adds a tangible Premium Economy feature, not a fleet standard
pages.why: A physical product feature is the claim, so the photograph leads and the specification follows under it

anchors.photo: Passengers using the Emirates A350 electric Premium Economy seats, September 2026

pages.title: 04 / The rivals are real
pages.why: Section structure

pages.title: Of five hub carriers, only Emirates is below its 2018 passenger count
pages.why: Whether Emirates' flat passenger count is its own or the market's is settled by indexing it against four hub carriers from the same base year

pages.title: Emirates earns the top network-airline margin while flying the emptiest seats of eleven
pages.why: The claim is that Emirates makes its margin by price rather than fill, which only shows when size, load factor and margin are read for the same eleven airlines on one axis

pages.title: Emirates flies the world's largest widebody fleet, 35 aircraft more than Qatar
pages.why: The claim is Emirates' place in the whole field of widebody operators, so twenty are sorted with Emirates marked

pages.title: Headline destination counts hide incompatible network definitions
pages.why: Each carrier's network claim needs its evidence and the reason it cannot be ranked, one carrier to a row

pages.title: Qatar pairs a larger published city count with premium leadership, but not with scale
pages.why: Qatar is the countercase to the whole deck, and weighing it is reasoning across several measures rather than one exhibit

pages.title: Qatar's 160 firm Boeing orders are mostly 787s, a different bet from Emirates' 777X
pages.why: Two orderbooks are compared by what they are made of, and the difference in mix is the claim

pages.title: Etihad is growing fastest: 21% more capacity, fuller aircraft and more seats in 2026
pages.why: Etihad's challenge has four separate signs - capacity, fill, profit and 2026 momentum - each with its own number, read down the page as a diagnosis

pages.title: Abu Dhabi and Doha each have more than 10 million passengers of terminal room
pages.why: Two airports' throughput and terminal capacity are four measured numbers, and the headroom between them is the claim

pages.title: Nearly half of Saudi airport traffic is domestic, so Saudia serves a different mission
pages.why: Three numbers carry the claim - the Saudi total, its domestic share and Saudia's fleet - over the Gulf airports that set them in scale

pages.title: Riyadh Air's 14 listed outstations span four regions, half of them in Asia
pages.why: Where Riyadh Air flies and how big its network is are two cuts of one question - how far it overlaps Emirates today - and each needs its own panel

pages.title: Riyadh Air moved from firm orders to 14 listed outstations in under two years
pages.why: Riyadh Air's build-out is a sequence of dated steps from orders to service, so it is drawn in time order

pages.title: A new Dammam carrier and flynas widen Saudi low-cost competition
pages.why: The new Dammam carrier and flynas are parallel low-cost threats, each read on its own card with the same measures

pages.title: 05 / The next decade
pages.why: Section structure

pages.title: Riyadh Air and flynas order far beyond their fleets; only Qatar matches Emirates' widebodies
pages.why: The next decade's capacity is set by fleets and order books together, so eight Gulf carriers are read on fleet, widebodies and orders on one axis

pages.title: The 777X has a 2027 programme aim, not an Emirates delivery date
pages.why: The 777X question is when, so the programme's dates and the airline's bridge are drawn on one time axis

pages.title: Saudi policy targets 2.3 times its 2025 airport traffic by 2030
pages.why: One ratio carries the claim - how far the 2030 target sits above 2025 traffic - and the column says what it would take

pages.title: IATA expects Middle East airlines to lose US$4.3bn in 2026 after a US$7.2bn profit
pages.why: The regional outlook is eight measures across two years and two regions, looked up rather than plotted

pages.title: Qatar closed most of the gap, but needs 8.4% yearly growth to draw level
pages.why: Qatar's actual passengers and the path it would need are one series over six years, and the gap between them is the claim

pages.title: The preferred airline changes with the decision being made
pages.why: The answer changes with the decision maker, so each decision is a row with its evidence, its preferred airline drawn as its mark, and the condition on it
highlight: 11.4m more passengers on the matched March year

pages.title: Four dated checks can reverse the Emirates case; the fleet check is at risk
pages.why: Four dated checks are each judged on one status - holding or at risk - and the one at-risk row is the finding

pages.title: Emirates is best positioned to lead, if execution matches the assets
pages.why: The close restates the answer as the conditions a reader should watch, one to an item
